docs.title: Embedded Systems I
docs.text:
This log documents the lab sessions for my Embedded Systems I course. Each entry covers a single session: the goal for that day, the hardware setup, the code written to meet it, and a short video showing the circuit actually working on the board.

The sessions build progressively on the RP2350 (Raspberry Pi Pico 2), moving from basic digital outputs (blinking and controlling individual LEDs) to digital inputs (reading push-buttons to reproduce logic gates and control on-board LEDs), and will continue expanding into more advanced peripherals — timers, PWM, analog inputs, communication protocols, and interrupts — as the course progresses.

Beyond the code and results, each entry also includes a short reflection on what went wrong during the session and what I learned from debugging it, along with any open questions I still have going into the next class. The goal is not just to keep a record of finished exercises, but to track my own understanding of embedded systems concepts as it develops throughout the semester.

docs.title: LDR + Electret on ADC0, Potentiometer Angle and NTC Temperature on Two Channels
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Use the RP2350 ADC on the Pico 2 W to read an LDR (EMA-filtered, shown in volts and as a 0–100 % light level) and an electret microphone (fixed raw threshold for "high noise") on ADC0, and then read a potentiometer (ADC1, mapped to 0–270°) and an NTC thermistor (ADC0, converted to °C with the Beta equation) in the same loop by switching the input channel.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
The RP2350 ADC is 12-bit with VREF = 3.3 V, so:

  • 1 LSB = 3.3 V / 4096 ≈ 0.806 mV V = raw · 3.3 / 4095
  • LDR level: Nivel = (y − LDR_MIN) · 100 / (LDR_MAX − LDR_MIN), with LDR_MIN = 9 and LDR_MAX = 3600 taken from the darkest and brightest raw values I saw before writing the code. Covered → ≈ 0 %; flashlight on top → high, but < 100 % (the flashlight was never pointed perfectly into the LDR).
  • EMA filter: y = α·x + (1 − α)·y with α = 1/16. At one sample every 100 ms, the time constant is ≈ Ts / α = 0.1 s · 16 = 1.6 s, so after a sudden light change the filtered value should only reach ~63 % of the jump after ~1.6 s and ~95 % after ~4.8 s. I expect Filtro to visibly lag Raw.
  • Electret threshold: the mic signal is biased around mid-scale (3.3 V / 2 = 1.65 V ≈ 2048). The threshold 2110 is 2110 · 3.3 / 4095 ≈ 1.70 V, i.e. ~62 LSB (~50 mV) above the bias point, so only a reasonably loud sound should print "Ruido alto".
  • Potentiometer angle: grados = ema · 270 / 4095, so each LSB is worth 270 / 4095 ≈ 0.066°. Ends of travel → 0° and 270°; wiper in the middle (raw ≈ 2048) → ≈ 135°.
  • NTC temperature: with the Beta equation (β = 3950, T0 = 25 °C = 298.15 K) and the NTC in a divider with a resistor equal to its nominal value, 25 °C should read raw ≈ 2048. Since the NTC resistance drops when it heats up and it sits on the low side of the divider, I expect hotter → lower raw value and colder → higher raw value. The same α = 1/16 EMA is used on both channels, so a step should need ~16 samples to reach ~63 % of the change.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: LDR_GPIO_PIN = GP26 → LDR_ADC_INPUT = ADC0. The same pin/channel is used for the electret (one sensor at a time, separate programs). In the pot + NTC program: GP27 → ADC1 (Pot_INPUT) and GP26 → ADC0 (Temp_INPUT).
  • LDR: voltage divider between 3.3 V and GND, midpoint to GP26. The reading goes up with light, so the LDR is on the 3.3 V side and the fixed resistor on the GND side.
  • Electret: electret capsule with its bias resistor, a coupling capacitor and a resistor divider that centers the signal around mid-supply before GP26.
  • Potentiometer + NTC (simulated in Wokwi): the pot wiper goes to GP27 (ADC1) and the analog output of the NTC temperature module goes to GP26 (ADC0); both take 3.3 V and GND from the Pico 2. The temperature is changed with the sensor's slider inside the simulator.
  • Non-default: none. adc_gpio_init() disables the digital input buffer and pulls on each analog pin; ADC in free single-shot mode (adc_read()), default 150 MHz clk_sys. USB serial monitor at 115200 baud.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Initialized the ADC (adc_init, adc_gpio_init(26), adc_select_input(0)) and printed raw values to find the dark/bright extremes of the LDR → used them as LDR_MIN = 9 and LDR_MAX = 3600.
  2. Added the EMA filter from the course notes (α = 0.0625), seeded with the first sample so it doesn't start from 0.
  3. Converted the filtered value to volts and to a percentage, and printed Raw | Filtro | Voltaje | Nivel every 100 ms.
  4. Recorded a demo: hands covering the LDR, then uncovered (room light), then a phone flashlight on top and moving away → adc_ldr_demo.mp4 (audio removed).
  5. Swapped the LDR for the electret front end and flashed adcmicrosencillo.c, which prints the raw value every 100 ms and labels it "Ruido alto" when raw > 2110, otherwise "Ruido normal".
  6. Built pot_temp.c in Wokwi to read two sensors in one loop: adc_select_input(1) for the pot, then adc_select_input(0) for the NTC, each one with its own EMA. The pot is mapped to grados = ema · 270 / 4095 and the NTC is converted to °C with the Beta equation (β = 3950, T0 = 25 °C). The loop runs every 10 ms.
  7. While recording the serial monitor, moved the NTC slider (18.8 → 80 → −24 °C) and turned the pot through its range → adc_pot_temp_demo.mp4.

Spot-check of the conversion with E4: 2397 · 3.3 / 4095 = 1.93 V ✔ and (2429 − 9) · 100 / 3591 = 67 % ✔ — the printed values match the formulas.

Potentiometer + NTC (Wokwi):

# File What it shows Reading on the serial monitor E6 adc_pot_temp_demo.mp4 ~0:01: NTC at the default 24 °C, pot at its maximum NTC raw = 2093 → 24.00 °C; pot raw = 4095 → 270° E7 adc_pot_temp_demo.mp4 ~0:03: slider moved up to 80.0 °C NTC raw = 461 → 80.04 °C E8 adc_pot_temp_demo.mp4 ~0:05: slider moved down to −24.0 °C raw = 3813, ema = 3734 → 3744 → −19.70 / −20.20 °C (EMA not settled yet) E9 adc_pot_temp_demo.mp4 ~0:08: NTC settled at −24.0 °C, pot around the middle NTC raw = 3813 → −23.98 °C; pot raw = 1941, ema = 1949 → 128° E10 adc_pot_temp_demo.mp4 ~0:11: pot turned all the way down raw = 0, ema = 368 → 345 → 323, angle = 24 → 22 → 21° (EMA going down) E11 adc_pot_temp_demo.mp4 ~0:14 and ~0:17: two more pot positions raw = 1533 → 101°; raw = 4078 → 268°

Spot-check with E7: 4095 / 461 − 1 = 7.883, ln(1 / 7.883) = −2.065, 1 / (−2.065 / 3950 + 1 / 298.15) = 353.19 K = 80.04 °C ✔. For the pot, E11 gives 1533 · 270 / 4095 = 101.1 → 101° ✔. Once the EMA settles the NTC reading stays within ~0.05 °C of the slider (E6, E7, E9), and the raw value drops when the temperature goes up (E7 vs E8), which confirms the prediction that the NTC is on the low side of the divider. In E10 each new EMA value is 368 · 15/16 = 345 and 345 · 15/16 = 323, exactly the α = 1/16 decay.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• Wiring error on the temperature sensor: the temperature sensor was connected wrong the first time, so it didn't give a valid reading and we had to check the wiring again before it worked.
  • No instrumented electret, so only a simple noise detector: we didn't buy the electret module with its own amplifier, so we only had the bare capsule with a basic bias/divider front end. Its signal is small, so instead of actually measuring sound level we built a simple noise detector: one raw sample compared against a fixed threshold (2110, ≈ 1.70 V) that prints "Ruido alto" / "Ruido normal".
  • Calibrating the potentiometer reading took some effort: it took several attempts to make the pot reading cover its whole range, until the raw values 0–4095 lined up with the real ends of the potentiometer (0° and 270°).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Shared setup code (same ADC initialization in the three programs — only the channels and the loop body change):

#include "pico/stdlib.h"
#include "hardware/adc.h"
#include <math.h>        // log() for the NTC Beta equation

#define LDR_GPIO_PIN   26   // GP26 -> ADC0 (LDR / electret / NTC)
#define LDR_ADC_INPUT  0
#define Temp_INPUT     0    // ADC0 -> GP26
#define Pot_INPUT      1    // ADC1 -> GP27
#define LDR_MIN        9
#define LDR_MAX        3600
#define BETA           3950.0

const float alpha = 0.0625f;   // EMA weight = 1/16

stdio_init_all();
adc_init();
adc_gpio_init(26);             // analog mode on GP26 (no digital buffer, no pulls)
adc_gpio_init(27);             // only in pot_temp.c
adc_select_input(LDR_ADC_INPUT);

LDR — EMA filter + conversion (Fotorresistencia.c)

uint16_t x = adc_read();                       // 0..4095
if (!y_init) { y = (float)x; y_init = true; }  // first sample seeds the filter
else          y = alpha * (float)x + (1.0f - alpha) * y;   // alpha = 1/16

uint16_t y_u16 = (uint16_t)(y + 0.5f);         // round the filtered value
float voltaje  = (y_u16 * 3.3f) / 4095.0f;
int porcentaje = ((y_u16 - LDR_MIN) * 100) / (LDR_MAX - LDR_MIN);

Electret — fixed threshold (adcmicrosencillo.c)

uint16_t m = adc_read();
if (m > 2110) printf("Raw=%u | Ruido alto\n", m);    // ~1.70 V, ~62 LSB above mid-scale
else          printf("Raw=%u | Ruido normal\n", m);
sleep_ms(100);

Potentiometer + NTC — two channels in one loop (pot_temp.c)

// Channel 1: potentiometer (GP27 -> ADC1)
adc_select_input(Pot_INPUT);
uint16_t xp = adc_read();
p = alpha * (float)xp + (1.0f - alpha) * p;          // EMA of the pot
uint16_t grados = (uint16_t)(p + 0.5f) * 270 / 4095;  // 0..270 degrees

// Channel 0: NTC thermistor (GP26 -> ADC0)
adc_select_input(Temp_INPUT);
uint16_t xt = adc_read();
t = alpha * (float)xt + (1.0f - alpha) * t;          // EMA of the NTC
double a = (double)(uint16_t)(t + 0.5f);
float temperatura = (float)(1.0 / (log(1.0 / (4095.0 / a - 1.0)) / BETA
                    + 1.0 / 298.15) - 273.15);       // Beta equation, T0 = 25 °C -> °C

docs.title: Open question
docs.text: The microphone code compares a single raw sample against NOISE_THRESHOLD = 2110. Would the peak-to-peak value or the RMS over a window of samples classify the noise more reliably than one sample?

docs.title: Practical Exam — 3x3 Lights-Out Puzzle with Bitwise State and Interrupts
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Build a Lights-Out–style puzzle on a 3×3 LED/button grid, where pressing a button toggles a plus-shaped set of neighboring LEDs, the whole board is tracked as a single bit-packed integer, and a dedicated button restarts the game at any moment via a hardware interrupt.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin mapping: GP2–GP10 drive the 9-LED grid (MASK_LED = 0x1FF << 2); GP11–GP19 are the 9 grid buttons (MASK_BTN = 0x1FF << 11); GP20 is the restart button. All ten buttons use internal pull-up resistors.
  • Unlike the roulette lab's rising-edge interrupts, here the interrupt is set on GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL — the moment the button goes down — since the win/lose check needs to react instantly to the press itself, not to its release.
  • The exam required: the board state in a single integer, every board operation done with bitwise operators only, no timer peripherals, restart served by interrupt (never polled), a self-written RNG (shifts + XOR, no rand()), every interrupt-shared variable marked volatile, and restart working from any state — including mid-victory-blink.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Wired the 9-LED grid on GP2–GP10, 9 grid buttons on GP11–GP19, and a restart button on GP20, all with internal pull-ups.
  2. Packed the entire board into one uint16_t, where bit i represents LED i in row-major order (0 1 2 / 3 4 5 / 6 7 8).
  3. Precomputed a PLUS_MASK[9] array so that applying a move is a single XOR against the pressed button's mask — this also makes every randomly generated starting board guaranteed solvable, since XOR is its own inverse.
  4. Wrote a self-contained xorshift32 RNG (only shifts and XOR) seeded at boot and re-mixed with the exact microsecond timestamp on every press, and used it to generate a starting board with generar_tablero().
  5. Wrote one shared interrupt callback that routes all ten pins: grid buttons XOR their PLUS_MASK into board, while the restart pin regenerates the board and clears the win flag unconditionally, with per-pin debounce done by comparing time_us_64() timestamps.

docs.title: Exercise — Bit-packed board with interrupt-driven moves and restart
docs.text:
#include "pico/stdlib.h"
#include "hardware/structs/sio.h"
#include "hardware/gpio.h"
#include <stdio.h>

#define LED_BASE     2
#define N_LEDS       9
#define BTN_BASE     11
#define N_BTN        9
#define RESTART_PIN  20

// Tiempo minimo entre dos pulsaciones del mismo boton para
// considerarlas distintas (filtra el rebote mecanico). Solo lee
// el contador libre de tiempo, no configura ningun timer.
#define DEBOUNCE_US  30000

const uint32_t MASK_LED = 0x1FF << LED_BASE;
const uint32_t MASK_BTN = 0x1FF << BTN_BASE;

// Estado del tablero: un solo entero, bit i = LED i encendido
static volatile uint16_t board = 0;
static volatile bool gane = false;

static uint32_t rng_state = 1;
static uint64_t ultimo_evt[N_BTN] = {0};
static uint64_t ultimo_evt_restart = 0;

// RNG propio (xorshift): solo shifts y XOR, nada de rand()
static inline uint32_t xorshift32(uint32_t *state)
{
    uint32_t x = *state;
    x ^= x << 13;
    x ^= x >> 17;
    x ^= x << 5;
    *state = x;
    return x;
}

// Mascaras "plus" precalculadas: aplicar un movimiento = una XOR
static const uint16_t PLUS_MASK[N_LEDS] = {
    0x00B, 0x017, 0x026,
    0x059, 0x0BA, 0x134,
    0x0C8, 0x1D0, 0x1A0
};

static void dibujar_tablero(void)
{
    sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK_LED;
    sio_hw->gpio_set = ((uint32_t)board) << LED_BASE;
}

// Genera un tablero siempre resoluble: XOR es su propio inverso
static uint16_t generar_tablero(void)
{
    uint16_t nuevo = 0;
    int n = 5 + (xorshift32(&rng_state) % 6);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
        int idx = xorshift32(&rng_state) % N_LEDS;
        nuevo ^= PLUS_MASK[idx];
    }
    if (nuevo == 0) nuevo = PLUS_MASK[4];
    return nuevo;
}

static void gpio_callback(uint gpio, uint32_t events)
{
    uint64_t ahora = time_us_64();
    rng_state ^= (uint32_t)ahora;

    if (gpio == RESTART_PIN)
    {
        // El restart funciona en cualquier momento, incluso en victoria
        if ((events & GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL) &&
            (ahora - ultimo_evt_restart > DEBOUNCE_US))
        {
            ultimo_evt_restart = ahora;
            board = generar_tablero();
            gane = false;
            dibujar_tablero();
            printf("RESTART -> tablero 0x%03X\n", board);
        }
        gpio_acknowledge_irq(gpio, events);
        return;
    }

    int idx = gpio - BTN_BASE;
    if (idx < 0 || idx >= N_BTN)
    {
        gpio_acknowledge_irq(gpio, events);
        return;
    }

    // Mientras gane == true, los botones de la grid ya no alteran el tablero
    if ((events & GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL) && !gane &&
        (ahora - ultimo_evt[idx] > DEBOUNCE_US))
    {
        ultimo_evt[idx] = ahora;
        board ^= PLUS_MASK[idx];
        printf("Boton %d -> 0x%03X\n", idx, board);

        if (board == 0)
        {
            gane = true;
            printf("BLACKOUT! Ganaste\n");
        }
        dibujar_tablero();
    }

    gpio_acknowledge_irq(gpio, events);
}

int main(void)
{
    stdio_init_all();

    rng_state = (uint32_t)time_us_32() | 1u;

    for (int i = 0; i < N_LEDS; i++)
        gpio_init(LED_BASE + i);
    sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = MASK_LED;

    for (int i = 0; i < N_BTN; i++)
    {
        gpio_init(BTN_BASE + i);
        gpio_pull_up(BTN_BASE + i);
    }
    gpio_init(RESTART_PIN);
    gpio_pull_up(RESTART_PIN);
    sio_hw->gpio_oe_clr = MASK_BTN | (1u << RESTART_PIN);

    board = generar_tablero();
    dibujar_tablero();

    gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback(BTN_BASE, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true, &gpio_callback);
    for (int i = 1; i < N_BTN; i++)
        gpio_set_irq_enabled(BTN_BASE + i, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(RESTART_PIN, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);

    while (true)
    {
        if (gane)
        {
            sio_hw->gpio_set = MASK_LED;
            sleep_ms(150);
            if (!gane) continue;
            sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK_LED;
            sleep_ms(150);
        }
        else
        {
            tight_loop_contents();
        }
    }
}

docs.title: DS1307 RTC and MPU6050 Sharing One Bus (Wokwi)
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Use i2c0 on the Pico 2 as the only master of a bus shared by two slaves — a DS1307 real-time clock (time and date) and an MPU6050 (acceleration, angular rate and temperature) — reading each one with a register-pointer write followed by a repeated START and a read, and printing the values over USB serial.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
• Addresses: the DS1307 has a fixed 7-bit address 0x68, and the MPU6050 also answers at 0x68 when AD0 is low. With both on the same SDA/SCL the replies would collide, so I expect to need AD0 = 1 → MPU6050 at 0x69.
  • DS1307: registers 0x00…0x06 hold seconds, minutes, hours, day of week, date, month and year in BCD, so printing each byte with %02x should already show the decimal digits (e.g. 0x59 → "59"). With one print every 2 s, the seconds should advance in steps of 2 and roll over correctly into the next minute.
  • MPU6050: a single 14-byte burst from 0x3B returns ax, ay, az, temp, gx, gy, gz as big-endian signed 16-bit values. With the default ranges:
    • acceleration: a = raw / 16384 g (±2 g)
    • angular rate: ω = raw / 131 °/s (±250 °/s)
    • temperature: T = raw / 340 + 36.53 °C
  • Negative readings should come out negative only if each pair of bytes is cast to int16_t before converting; otherwise they would wrap to large positive numbers.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: SDA = GP4, SCL = GP5 (i2c0), shared by both modules. DS1307 → 0x68; MPU6050 → 0x69 (AD0 tied to 3V3).
  • Both modules powered from the Pico's 3V3 and GND.
  • Simulated in Wokwi:
  • Non-default: none on the Pico side. Bus at 100 kHz (standard mode, the DS1307's maximum) with the RP2350 internal pull-ups instead of external resistors; MPU6050 left at its default ±2 g / ±250 °/s ranges; default 150 MHz clk_sys.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Connected SDA and SCL of both modules to GP4 and GP5 and tied the MPU6050's AD0 to 3V3 to move it to 0x69.
  2. Initialized i2c0 at 100 kHz, set GP4/GP5 to GPIO_FUNC_I2C and enabled their pull-ups.
  3. RTC: wrote the register pointer 0x00 with nostop = true (repeated START), read 7 bytes and printed time and date in hex, since the registers are already BCD.
  4. MPU6050: same sequence from register 0x3B, read 14 bytes, joined each high/low pair into an int16_t and converted it to g, °/s and °C.
  5. Ran the simulation, moved the MPU6050 sliders in Wokwi while the serial monitor was printing, and recorded it → i2c_wokwi_demo.mp4 (audio removed).

Download i2c_wokwi_demo.mp4

Spot-check, working the formulas backwards to the raw register values: 52.2 °C → (52.2 − 36.53) · 340 ≈ 5328 and −14.2 °C → (−14.2 − 36.53) · 340 ≈ −17248; −1.40 g → −1.40 · 16384 ≈ −22938; −170 °/s → −170 · 131 = −22270. All of them fit inside a signed 16-bit range (±32767), and the negative ones only print as negative because of the int16_t cast ✔. The seconds in E1 move by exactly 2 per line and roll from 59 to 01 into the next minute ✔, and every line of E2/E3 shows both devices still answering on the shared bus.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• Two slaves at the same address: with AD0 left low, the MPU6050 also sat at 0x68, the same as the DS1307, so we couldn't tell which device was answering. Tying AD0 to 3V3 moved the MPU6050 to 0x69 and fixed it.
  • Wrong return codes in the MPU error message: the MPU6050 error check was copied from the RTC block and was still printing the RTC's return values. We changed it to use the MPU's own i2c_write_blocking / i2c_read_blocking results. It never showed up in the demo because in Wokwi both devices always acknowledged.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Shared setup code (bus and addresses — both devices are read with the same pointer-write + repeated-START pattern):

#define I2C_PORT     i2c0
#define SDA_PIN      4
#define SCL_PIN      5
#define DS1307_ADDR  0x68
#define MPU_ADDR     0x69          // AD0 = 3V3 (0x68 would collide with the DS1307)

i2c_init(I2C_PORT, 100 * 1000);    // 100 kHz, standard mode
gpio_set_function(SDA_PIN, GPIO_FUNC_I2C);
gpio_set_function(SCL_PIN, GPIO_FUNC_I2C);
gpio_pull_up(SDA_PIN);             // internal pull-ups instead of external resistors
gpio_pull_up(SCL_PIN);

DS1307 — 7 BCD registers from 0x00

uint8_t reg = 0x00, rtc[7];
i2c_write_blocking(I2C_PORT, DS1307_ADDR, &reg, 1, true);       // pointer -> 0x00, keep the bus (repeated START)
int r_rtc = i2c_read_blocking(I2C_PORT, DS1307_ADDR, rtc, 7, false);

if (r_rtc == 7)                                                  // BCD printed in hex = decimal digits
    printf("RTC %02x:%02x:%02x  %02x/%02x/%02x\n",
           rtc[2], rtc[1], rtc[0] & 0x7F, rtc[4], rtc[5], rtc[6]);

MPU6050 — 14-byte burst from 0x3B

uint8_t mreg = 0x3B, d[14];
int w_mpu = i2c_write_blocking(I2C_PORT, MPU_ADDR, &mreg, 1, true);
int r_mpu = i2c_read_blocking(I2C_PORT, MPU_ADDR, d, 14, false);
if (w_mpu < 0 || r_mpu < 0) printf("MPU error: w=%d r=%d\n", w_mpu, r_mpu);   // MPU's own codes

int16_t ay   = (int16_t)(d[2]  << 8 | d[3]);    // cast keeps the sign
int16_t az   = (int16_t)(d[4]  << 8 | d[5]);

docs.title: LED Fade, Clock Divider and an 8-Key Piano (Predict vs Measure)
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Predict a PWM signal's frequency and duty from clk_sys, the clock divider and TOP and check it on the oscilloscope (Part 1, LED), then use the same formula backwards to play notes on a speaker with an 8-key PWM piano (Part 2).

docs.title: Part 1 — LED Fade, Clock Divider and Fixed Duty
Prediction
docs.text:
A PWM slice counts 0 … TOP at clk_sys / div, so:

  • f_PWM = f_clk / (div · (TOP + 1)) duty = level / (TOP + 1) +W = duty · T
  • Course example (F_PWM_HZ = 2000, TOP = 1023, f_clk = 150 MHz): div = 150 MHz / (2000 · 1024) = 73.24 → f = 2.000 kHz, T = 500.0 µs
  • DIV_10 (div = 10, TOP = 4095): 150 MHz / (10 · 4096) → f = 3.662 kHz, T = 273.1 µs
  • DIV_1 (div = 1, TOP = 4095): 150 MHz / (1 · 4096) → f = 36.62 kHz, T = 27.31 µs
  • Fixed duty at 2 kHz, TOP = 1023: 35 % → +W ≈ 175 µs, 87 % → +W ≈ 435 µs, 20 % → +W ≈ 100 µs
  • Fade (step = 8, sleep_ms(5)): the level sweeps 0 → TOP → 0 like a triangle, so a random scope snapshot sees a roughly uniform duty between 0 and 100 %: mean ≈ 50 %, σ ≈ 100 / √12 = 28.9 %. Ramp time ≈ (TOP / 8) · 5 ms = 0.64 s for TOP = 1023 (2.56 s for TOP = 4095).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: LED_PIN = GP2 → LED (with series resistor) and scope CH1; scope ground → a Pico GND pin.
  • Photo of the breadboard: not taken this session (Pico 2 W, one LED on GP2, probe on GP2 / GND).
  • Non-default: none. Default 150 MHz clk_sys (the course text says 125 MHz, but the example code hard-codes 150 MHz — with 125 MHz the same divider would give ≈ 1.67 kHz instead of 2 kHz). Scope at 5 MS/s (200 µs/div) for the 2 kHz runs, 10 MS/s and 100 MS/s for the faster ones; 10k points, trigger on CH1 rising edge at 920 mV.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Flashed the course pwm_led.c (fade, 2 kHz, TOP = 1023) and probed GP2 at 200 µs/div with Frequency / Period / +Width / Duty measurements → E1–E3.
  2. Did the divider math by hand with a calculator and left it as an integer (div = 73 instead of 73.24), reflashed and measured again → E2, E3.
  3. Changed TOP to 4095 and set the divider to 10 (DIV_10), then to 1 (DIV_1), keeping the fade → E4, E5.
  4. Went back to 2 kHz (TOP = 1023, div = 73), turned the fade off and wrote a fixed level for 35 %, 87 % and 20 % duty → E6–E8.
  5. Compared every Value/Mean reading with the formula above.

Lowering the divider ×10 multiplies the frequency ×10 (E4 → E5) without changing the duty behavior; TOP trades frequency for resolution.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• 2.002 / 2.007 kHz instead of 2.000 kHz: the prediction said exactly 2 kHz, but E1 reads 2.002 kHz and the later runs 2.006–2.007 kHz. Two causes, both in the divider:
    • With the course float (E1): the RP2350 stores the divider as 8 integer + 4 fractional bits (steps of 1/16), and pwm_set_clkdiv() truncates the float, so 73.24 becomes 73.1875 → 2001.5 Hz.
    • With our calculator value (E2–E8): we did the math by hand and left the divider as the integer 73, dropping the 0.24 → 150 MHz / (73 · 1024) = 2006.6 Hz, i.e. +0.33 %. The scope matched the divider we actually wrote, not the 2 kHz we wanted.
    • Fix: pick TOP and div so the divider is exact — e.g. TOP = 999, div = 75 → 150 MHz / (75 · 1000) = exactly 2000 Hz — or compute the real frequency from the stored divider instead of the requested one.
  • Polluted statistics: E2/E3 show Min period = 350 ns and Max frequency = 2.857 MHz, which are impossible for a 2 kHz PWM. They came from glitches while reflashing / reconnecting the probe, and the statistics were never reset. We trusted only the Value and Mean columns; next time press Reset Statistics after the signal settles.
  • "Value" duty means nothing during the fade: E1–E5 show duties of 17 %, 60 %, 79 %, 95 %… depending on when the snapshot was taken. For the fade, the useful numbers are Mean (≈ 50 %) and Std Dev (≈ 28.9 %), not Value.

pwm_set_chan_level(slice, chan, level);
pwm_set_enabled(slice, true);

docs.text:

  2. Wrote piano.c: TOP = 1023 fixed, a table NOTAS[8], and in the loop the first pressed key sets pwm_set_clkdiv(slice, f_clk / (NOTAS[i] · 1024)) and enables the slice; no key → slice disabled (silence).
  3. Added BTN_UP / BTN_DOWN to move the channel level in steps of 64 (6.25 % duty), clamped to 0 … TOP.
  4. Flashed it, played a few melodies across all 8 keys and recorded it with sound: img/pwm_piano_demo.mp4.

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• One key at a time (by design, but it surprised us): pressing two keys plays only the lower one, because the for loop breaks on the first pressed key and a slice can only produce one frequency. A chord would need a second slice/pin.
  • sleep_ms(150) in the volume buttons blocks the keys: while BTN_UP/BTN_DOWN is held, the loop only runs every ~155 ms, so the note keys respond late. It's acceptable for a demo; a timer/IRQ-based debounce (like Session 8) would fix it.
  • The "volume" buttons don't really change volume linearly: they change the duty. The loudest fundamental is at 50 % (level = 512); moving up or down from there makes the tone quieter and thinner, and at 0 % or 100 % (level 0 / TOP) there is no sound at all.

}

docs.title: Session- Repeating Timer on GP15 (Predict vs Measure)
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Generate a square wave on GP15 from an SDK repeating timer (no sleep_ms in the loop), predict its period, frequency and duty cycle from TOGGLE_MS, and check the prediction on the oscilloscope.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
The callback toggles GP15 once every TOGGLE_MS, so one full period is one HIGH plus one LOW:

  • T = 2 · TOGGLE_MS f = 1 / T = 1000 / (2 · TOGGLE_MS) Hz duty = 50 % (HIGH and LOW both last TOGGLE_MS)
  • TOGGLE_MS = 250 → HIGH = LOW = 250 ms, T = 500 ms, f = 1000 / 500 = 2.000 Hz
  • TOGGLE_MS = 10 → HIGH = LOW = 10 ms, T = 20 ms, f = 1000 / 20 = 50.00 Hz

With a negative delay (-TOGGLE_MS) the callbacks are scheduled start-to-start, so I expected no drift: at most a few µs of jitter from interrupt latency on each edge.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map: GP15 → scope CH1 (timer output); scope ground → a Pico GND pin only. GP14 (CH2 callback marker) was not used in these captures.
  • Photo of the breadboard: not taken this session (only the Pico and the probe on GP15 / GND).
  • Non-default: none. Default 150 MHz clk_sys, timer at its default 1 µs tick, no pulls, no external parts. Scope at 5 kS/s, 10k points, trigger on CH1 rising edge.

docs.text:
1. Copied the course repeating-timer code, set OUT_PIN = 15, TOGGLE_MS = 250, add_repeating_timer_ms(-TOGGLE_MS, …).
  2. Built and flashed; probed GP15 on CH1, 200 ms/div, added Frequency / Period / +Width / −Width measurements → E1.
  3. Changed TOGGLE_MS to 10, rebuilt and flashed.
  4. Zoomed in 50× (4 ms/div) on the 200 ms/div record → E2.
  5. Saved a second capture 3 s later to check repeatability → E3.

docs.title: Two-Pico Button/LED Mirror
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Connect two Pico 2 boards through UART0 so that pressing a button on one board turns on the matching LED on the other board, and releasing it turns that LED off — in both directions, with the same firmware on both boards.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin map (identical on both boards): TX_PIN=GP0 (UART0 TX), RX_PIN=GP1 (UART0 RX); Button_A=GP12, Button_B=GP13, Button_C=GP14; Led_A=GP16, Led_B=GP17, Led_C=GP18 (each LED with its series resistor).
  • Board-to-board wiring: GP0 (TX) of board 1 → GP1 (RX) of board 2, GP0 (TX) of board 2 → GP1 (RX) of board 1, and a shared GND between both breadboards.
  • Photo of the setup:
  • Non-default: internal pull-ups on the three buttons (gpio_pull_up), so a press reads 0. UART0 configured as 115200 baud, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, no parity (uart_set_format(UART_ID, 8, 1, UART_PARITY_NONE)). Default 150 MHz clk_sys, nothing else changed.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Wired 3 buttons (GP12–GP14) and 3 LEDs (GP16–GP18) on each breadboard, then crossed TX/RX between the two Picos and joined their grounds.
  2. Configured GP0/GP1 as GPIO_FUNC_UART and initialized uart0 at 115200 8N1.
  3. Defined a tiny protocol of one character per event: uppercase ('A', 'B', 'C') = button pressed → LED on; lowercase ('a', 'b', 'c') = button released → LED off.
  4. Used one flag per button so each letter is sent only once per press/release edge, and on the receive side read every byte available with while (uart_is_readable(...)), acting only on those six letters.
  5. Flashed the same program to both boards, tested every button in both directions and recorded a short demo (audio removed): img/uart_demo.mp4.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: # File What it shows E1 img/uart_demo.mp4 ~0:01–0:04: a button is pressed on the bottom board and the LED on the top board turns on while the button is held Board 2 → Board 1 direction works E2 img/uart_demo.mp4 ~0:05–0:09: a button is pressed on the top board and the matching LED on the bottom board turns on, then turns off on release Board 1 → Board 2 direction works, and the release (lowercase letter) turns it off

docs.title: What went wrong
docs.text:
• Letters sent over and over: the first version did if (gpio_get(Button_A) == 0) uart_putc(UART_ID, 'A'); inside the loop, so as long as the button was held it kept sending 'A' every 10 ms — the other board received a continuous stream instead of one event. Fix: add flag_a / flag_b / flag_c so the letter is sent only on the edge (when the button goes from released to pressed) and a lowercase letter only when it goes back.
  • LEDs turning off by themselves (else on the receiver): in that first version I only sent uppercase letters to turn LEDs on, and the receiver did if (c == 'A') gpio_put(Led_A, 1); else gpio_put(Led_A, 0);. On the terminal it looked like only my letters were arriving, but there were "gaps" where something else was received that didn't show (non-printable characters such as \r/\n, or simply the letter of a different button). Any byte that wasn't 'A' fell into the else and turned LED A off, even though I was still holding the button. Fix: send an explicit off command ('a', 'b', 'c') on release and remove the generic else — now each LED only changes when its own two letters arrive, and any other byte is ignored.

docs.text:
// --- SEND: only on edges (flag), not every loop iteration ---
if (gpio_get(Button_A) == 0 && flag_a == 0) {
    uart_putc(UART_ID, 'A');      // pressed
    flag_a = 1;
} else if (gpio_get(Button_A) == 1 && flag_a == 1) {
    uart_putc(UART_ID, 'a');      // released
    flag_a = 0;
}
...
// --- RECEIVE: only react to our own letters, no generic else ---
while (uart_is_readable(UART_ID)) {
    char c = uart_getc(UART_ID);
    if (c == 'A')      gpio_put(Led_A, 1);
    else if (c == 'a') gpio_put(Led_A, 0);   // any other byte is ignored
    ...
}
sleep_ms(10);

docs.title: Session 6 — Two-Button Logic Gates and a Shifting LED
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Configure two push-buttons with internal pull-downs as digital inputs, use them to emulate OR, AND, and XOR logic on a single LED, and then reuse the same buttons to shift a lit LED across four positions.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin mapping: GP2 drives the LED used for the OR/AND/XOR exercises; GP6 and GP7 are the two push-buttons, both configured as inputs through gpio_pull_down().
  • For the shifting exercise, the LED output expands to a 4-bit bus on GP2–GP5 (MASK_LED = 0xF << 2), while the buttons stay on GP6 and GP7.
  • Important detail: since these buttons rely on internal pull-down resistors, pressing a button drives the line high (1), unlike the pull-up wiring used in the previous session — no ! negation is needed here.
  • stdio_init_all() and a printf() call are used in the OR/AND/XOR versions to print the raw button-mask value to the serial console on each loop iteration, which was useful for confirming the readings while debugging.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Wired a single LED on GP2 (plus GP3–GP5 for the shifting exercise) and two push-buttons on GP6 and GP7, each configured as an input with gpio_pull_down().
  2. Built three variations of essentially the same program — same setup, only the condition evaluating the two button states changes — so the LED behaves as an OR, an AND, and an XOR gate.
  3. Wrote a fourth program that uses one button to advance a position counter and the other to move it back, lighting only the LED at the current position and wrapping around at both ends of the 4-bit bus.
  4. Captured each behavior on video as supporting evidence.

docs.title: Exercise 1 — AND gate
docs.text:
The LED only turns on when both buttons are pressed at the same time (with pull-downs, "pressed" reads as 1, so no negation is required).

#include "pico/stdlib.h"
#include "hardware/structs/sio.h"
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    stdio_init_all();

    const uint32_t MASK_LED = 1u<< 2;
    const uint32_t MASK_BOTONES = (1u << 6) | (1u << 7);

    gpio_init(2);
    gpio_init(6);
    gpio_init(7);

    sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = MASK_LED;
    sio_hw->gpio_oe_clr = MASK_BOTONES;

    gpio_pull_down(6);
    gpio_pull_down(7);

    while (true) {

        uint32_t entaadas = sio_hw->gpio_in;


        int resultado = (entaadas & MASK_BOTONES);
        printf("Botones: %d\n", resultado);
        if (entaadas & 1<<6 && entaadas & 1<<7) {
            sio_hw->gpio_set = MASK_LED;
        } else {
            sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK_LED;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Exercise 4 — Shift the lit LED left/right
docs.text:
One button (GP6) advances a counter variable and the other (GP7) decreases it; only the LED at position counter is lit on the 4-bit bus (GP2–GP5). Two separate flags, f1 and f2, latch each button independently so a press only increments/decrements once instead of repeating while held, and the counter wraps at both edges (0–3). A short sleep_ms(15) at the end of the loop acts as simple debounce.

#include "pico/stdlib.h"
#include "hardware/structs/sio.h"
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    stdio_init_all();

    const uint32_t MASK_LED = 0xF << 2;// bits 2,3,4,5 = 0b111100
    const uint32_t MASK_BOTONES = (1u << 6) | (1u << 7);

    gpio_init(2);
    gpio_init(3);
    gpio_init(4);
    gpio_init(5);
    gpio_init(6);
    gpio_init(7);

    sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = MASK_LED;
    sio_hw->gpio_oe_clr = MASK_BOTONES;

    gpio_pull_down(6);
    gpio_pull_down(7);

    int counter = 0;
    int f1= 0;
    int f2= 0;
while (true) {
        uint32_t entradas = sio_hw->gpio_in;
        int a = (entradas & (1u << 6)) != 0;
        int b = (entradas & (1u << 7)) != 0;

        // --- Botón 1: avanza ---
        if (a && !f1) {
            counter++;
            if (counter > 3) counter = 0;   // wrap 0..3
            f1 = 1;
        } else if (!a && f1) {
            f1 = 0;
        }

        // --- Botón 2: retrocede ---
        if (b && !f2) {
            counter--;
            if (counter < 0) counter = 3;   // wrap 0..3
            f2 = 1;
        } else if (!b && f2) {
            f2 = 0;
        }

        // --- Refresca LEDs cada vuelta ---
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK_LED;               // apaga todos
        sio_hw->gpio_set = (1u << (2 + counter));  // prende solo el actual

        sleep_ms(15); // debounce sencillo
    }
}

docs.title: Session — 5-LED Roulette Controlled by GPIO Interrupts
docs.text: Goal (one sentence): Build a 5-LED roulette that lights one LED at a time, controlled by hardware interrupts instead of polling, where one button checks for a win on the middle LED and a second button cycles the roulette speed.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pin mapping: GP2–GP6 drive the 5-LED bus (MASK_LED = 0x1F << 2); GP7 is the win/restart button; GP8 is the speed button. Both buttons use the internal pull-up (gpio_pull_up()), so each pin reads 1 when idle and drops to 0 on press.
  • Unlike polling-based labs, both buttons are read through hardware interrupts set on GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_RISE, so each callback fires the instant the button is released back up, not while it's held down.
  • Three variables are shared between the interrupts and the main loop — gane, counter, and vel — and all three are declared volatile, since a value written inside an interrupt could otherwise be cached and never show up in main().

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Wired the 5-LED bus on GP2–GP6 and two push-buttons on GP7 and GP8, both with internal pull-ups.
  2. Registered a single interrupt callback (the Pico SDK only allows one global callback per core) and wrote a router function, escoge_boton, that checks which pin fired and forwards it to the right handler.
  3. Wrote the main loop to run the roulette by polling only a counter variable — lighting 1u << (2 + counter) and advancing every vel milliseconds — while all button logic lives entirely in the interrupt handlers.

docs.title: Exercise — Win detection and speed control
docs.text:
#include "pico/stdlib.h"
#include "hardware/structs/sio.h"
#include "hardware/gpio.h"
#include <stdio.h>


#define BOTON_PIN 7  
#define BOTON_PIN2 8  


const uint32_t MASK_LED = 0x1F << 2;


volatile bool gane = false;  
volatile int counter = 0;  
volatile int vel = 500;  


void stop_callback(uint gpio, uint32_t events)
{

    if (gpio == BOTON_PIN && (events & GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_RISE))
    {
        printf("Botón de ganar presionado\n");

        if (!gane)
        {

            if (counter == 2)
            {
                printf("¡Ganaste! Empieza el parpadeo\n");
                gane = true;
            }
            else
            {

                printf("Fallaste, sigue jugando\n");
            }
        }
        else
        {
            printf("Reiniciando el juego\n");
            gane = false;  
            counter = 0;  
        }
    }


    gpio_acknowledge_irq(gpio, events);
}


void boton_velocidad(uint gpio, uint32_t events)
{
    if (gpio == BOTON_PIN2 && (events & GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_RISE))
    {
        printf("Botón de velocidad presionado\n");


        if (vel == 500)
        {
            vel = 250;
        }
        else if (vel == 250)
        {
            vel = 100;
        }
        else if (vel == 100)
        {
            vel = 500;
        }
    }

    gpio_acknowledge_irq(gpio, events);
}

void escoge_boton(uint gpio, uint32_t events)
{
    if (gpio == BOTON_PIN)
    {
        stop_callback(gpio, events);
    }
    else if (gpio == BOTON_PIN2)
    {
        boton_velocidad(gpio, events);
    }
}

int main(void)
{
    stdio_init_all();


    gpio_init(2);
    gpio_init(3);
    gpio_init(4);
    gpio_init(5);
    gpio_init(6);
    gpio_init(BOTON_PIN);
    gpio_init(BOTON_PIN2);


    sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = MASK_LED;


    sio_hw->gpio_oe_clr = (1u << BOTON_PIN) | (1u << BOTON_PIN2);

    // Pull-up: el pin normalmente está en "1" (alto), y baja a "0"
    // cuando presionas el botón (conecta a GND)
    gpio_pull_up(BOTON_PIN);
    gpio_pull_up(BOTON_PIN2);


    gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback(BOTON_PIN, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_RISE, true, &escoge_boton);


    gpio_set_irq_enabled(BOTON_PIN2, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_RISE, true);


    while (true)
    {
        if (gane)
        {

            sio_hw->gpio_set = MASK_LED;
            sleep_ms(200);
            sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK_LED;
            sleep_ms(200);

        }
        else
        {

            sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK_LED;  
            sio_hw->gpio_set = (1u << (2 + counter));  
            sleep_ms(vel);  

            printf("GPIO: %d \n", sio_hw->gpio_in);

            counter++;  
            if (counter > 4)  
                counter = 0;  
        }
    }
}
